clue.text: Scold or preach conversion

indicators.note: A conversion turns one thing into another without adding anything, which is exactly what happens to the letters it points at.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers 'or' as a choice between two ways of telling someone off. It is really the first two letters of the fodder — a joining word that turns out to be raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: To reproach someone is to tell them off for a fault, which is what scolding is; both verbs cover the same rebuke.

clue.text: Magazine's obligation to describe source of material

indicators.note: In geometry you describe a circle around a point, so this verb means to go round something rather than to depict it.

parts.note: a tie is a binding obligation — family ties, ties of duty

indicators.note: A source is where a thing starts, so what is wanted is the letter the following word starts from.

parts.note: the initial letter of Material

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is journalistic ethics — a reporter's duty to name a source — which is why nothing in it sounds like a set of letters being wrapped around one more.
explanation.definitionFit: Magazine → TIME: the definition names an actual title, the American weekly, rather than giving a synonym for the word magazine.

clue.text: What even number is divided by 5000?

indicators.note: To divide something is to split it in two, and the piece named next is what goes into the gap the split opens.

parts.note: par is the golfer's level score — being on par is being even
n is the mathematician's letter for any number you like
D is the Roman five hundred, O is a nought, so writing them together writes the figure out

explanation.walkthrough: Qaos writes numbers with letters twice in this grid — here and at 11 across — by putting a Roman numeral in front of a nought. Read the digits, not the arithmetic.
explanation.definitionFit: 'What?' and 'Pardon?' are the two things you say when you did not catch what somebody said, so one substitutes for the other exactly.

clue.text: Iron Lady's bored by acting Tory leader's 'soft touch'

indicators.note: bored by means pierced, so the second group of letters goes inside the first

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
her stands for a lady, the female pronoun
A is a dictionary abbreviation for acting, as in an acting rank

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher, the Iron Lady, is bored by a stand-in Conservative leader's gentle approach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron Lady' points to Thatcher but splits into the symbol for iron and the pronoun for a lady.
explanation.definitionFit: A feather is the proverbial light touch, so its brush is a soft touch.

clue.text: Country rejects American PR

indicators.note: To reject something is to throw it out, so the letter named after it is turned away from the word.

parts.note: the country on the Iberian peninsula
A is the standard abbreviation for American — this is what gets thrown out

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a diplomatic snub. The definition is two capital letters at the end of the clue, which is exactly where a solver's eye slides past them.
explanation.definitionFit: PR is public relations, and spin is the trade's own word for presenting a story in whichever light flatters the client most.

clue.text: 10 hide under end of divan, trembling

indicators.note: The end of a word is its final letter, the one it stops on.
Something trembling will not hold still, and letters that will not hold still are asking to be written down in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, nine letters
the letter divaN stops on

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the number 10, pointing at the answer to 10 across. Cross-references look like wordplay and are not: go and solve the other clue first.
explanation.definitionFit: 10 across is FREE, and to be unhindered is to be free of anything in your way — the obstruction sense of free rather than the no-charge one.

clue.text: Transfer money

definitions.meaning: moving from one train, account or job to another
the loose coins in a pocket, the small stuff a till hands back

explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue is nearly always two definitions: with no room for an indicator there is nowhere for wordplay to hide, so each word has to define on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are everyday but unrelated: the verb for swapping one thing for another, and the noun for the coins you are given back at a counter.

clue.text: Fine food store providing meals 50% off

indicators.note: A sale sign on the surface; underneath it means half the letters go, and it is the back half that leaves.

parts.note: a delicatessen, shortened the way every high street shortens it
providing meals for an event is catering — eight letters, and only the front four survive

explanation.walkthrough: Fine, food and store read as one shop-window phrase, and only the first word of it is the definition. That join is the clue's real trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine here means finely made rather than acceptable: fine bone china is delicate china, the sense of fine that describes workmanship.

clue.text: Wordplay by church magazine in the past

parts.note: a pun is wordplay at its plainest
CH is the standard crossword abbreviation for church

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke told in a pew, and it gives no hint that the answer is a magazine — or, for that matter, a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Punch was the British satirical weekly, founded in 1841 and closed in 2002, so the definition has to put it in the past tense.

clue.text: Release knot after cycling

indicators.note: cycling sends a letter round from one end of the word for knot to the other

parts.note: a reef is a type of knot, as in reef knot

explanation.surface: Someone frees a tangle once they've been out on a bike ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after cycling' moves the last letter of REEF to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To free a prisoner or animal is to let it go, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: 50 leave prayers over 10 school punishments?

indicators.note: over here means covering or lying across, so the remaining letters go around the number
to leave is to depart, so those letters drop out of the word for prayers

parts.note: devotions are acts of religious worship or prayers
read the figures one by one: 5 is V in Roman numerals and 0 looks like the letter O
ten is the number written in words

explanation.surface: Fifty worshippers walk out of a service with ten others.
explanation.walkthrough: The trick is reading 50 not as L but digit by digit, 5 and 0, which gives the Roman V and the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Detentions are periods of being kept back after lessons as discipline; the question mark flags that these are only an example of punishment.

clue.text: Lord caught being unproductive

indicators.note: To catch what somebody says is to hear it, so this is an ear-word — not, as the surface pretends, a cricket dismissal.

parts.note: the lowest rank in the peerage is a baron, and said out loud it comes out spelled the other way

explanation.walkthrough: There is cricket all through this puzzle, so 'caught' does a lot of work: it sounds like a dismissal and means an overheard word. BARON heard becomes BARREN.
explanation.definitionFit: Land that grows no crop is unproductive in the literal sense, and the word stretches by habit to any effort that yields nothing.

clue.text: Stopping official education ignoring tense

parts.note: the referee, the official who runs a match

indicators.note: To ignore something is to leave it out, so the letter it names is simply not written down.

parts.note: training is education of the practical sort
T is the grammarian's abbreviation for tense — this is the letter left out

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket has umpires, football has the REF, and crosswords use REF for any official at all. The surface, a school losing a lesson, has nothing to do with grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: To refrain from doing something is to hold back from it, which is stopping in the sense of stopping yourself rather than stopping a machine.

clue.text: Half of them plot to protect cricket match represented

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word is two letters, here the back half

parts.note: the second half of them

indicators.note: to protect is to surround, so the garden plot surrounds the cricket match

parts.note: a bed is a garden plot
ODI is a one-day international, a cricket match

explanation.surface: Half of a group plot to shield a cricket match from interference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plot' suggests a conspiracy, but it is a garden bed; ODI is the usual short form of a one-day international.
explanation.definitionFit: To embody an idea is to give it concrete form, so something embodied is represented in physical shape.

clue.text: Beauty product to go in container

indicators.note: Something told to go is being got rid of, and the joke is that what goes is the little word 'to' itself.

parts.note: the wrinkle-smoothing injection sold as a beauty treatment
these are the two letters that leave, and the clue names them by using the word

explanation.walkthrough: The instruction is hiding in plain sight: BOTOX loses the very word the clue used to tell it to go, and BOX is what is left standing.
explanation.definitionFit: A box is the plainest container in the language — four sides and a lid — which is why the definition is a single unglamorous noun.

clue.text: Prepare to deal in Harlem, maybe

definitions.note: The second definition works by example rather than synonym: 'maybe' warns you that Harlem names one particular dance, and you have to supply the word the dance and the card table share.
definitions.meaning: what a dealer does to the pack before the cards go out
the dance named after that New York district, and the 1963 hit song about it

explanation.walkthrough: Two senses, no letters moved: the card table on one side, Bob and Earl's Harlem Shuffle on the other. 'Maybe' is the flag that an example is standing in for a definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Riffling the pack before dealing is a shuffle, and a shuffle is also a dance step — the Harlem Shuffle being the famous one.

clue.text: Guided light

definitions.meaning: the past tense of lead: showed the way, went in front
the light-emitting diode now in every torch, bulb and standby indicator

explanation.walkthrough: A three-letter clue with no indicator is nearly always two definitions. The trap is reading 'light' as an adjective when it is a noun, and an acronym pretending to be a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Two unrelated things spelled the same way: the past tense of the verb 'lead', and the initials of the light-emitting diode.

clue.text: Ruler deports 1,000 to win vote, say

indicators.note: to deport is to expel from a country, so that letter is sent out of the ruler's word
to win here is to gain in exchange, so a new letter comes in where the old one left

parts.note: an empress is a female ruler of an empire
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
X is the mark made on a ballot paper to vote

explanation.surface: A dictator expels a thousand people in order to win an election.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deports' removes M from EMPRESS and 'to win' brings in X in its place.
explanation.definitionFit: To express a thought is to put it into words, so it is a synonym for state or utter.

clue.text: Foolish to steal ten pounds without a sound

indicators.note: to steal is to take in, so the foolish word holds the other letters

parts.note: silly means foolish

indicators.note: pounds means batters or beats, so the letters of ten are knocked about

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: It would be foolish to steal ten pounds while making no noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' looks like the money being stolen, but it is the verb: ten is beaten into ENT, which SILLY takes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Silently means making no noise at all, so it is acting without a sound.

clue.text: Take defensive position as grenade's thrown

definitions.note: The answer is a fencing master's command, not a verb phrase: 'take defensive position' describes what obeying it looks like, which is the closest English can get to translating it.

indicators.note: A thrown grenade lands where it lands, and letters thrown about land out of their original order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a soldier diving for cover and the answer is a fencer coming on guard. The enumeration (2,5) is the first hint that one word will not do.
explanation.definitionFit: 'En garde' is French for 'on guard', the call that tells a fencer to bring the blade up and cover themselves before the bout starts.

clue.text: Occasional cricket sides

definitions.note: The second definition names rather than translates: a cricket field is split into two halves with a name each, and the clue simply lists them in order.
definitions.meaning: happening now and then, with gaps in between
the field is divided either side of the batter's stance, and each half carries its own name

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, both defining. On the surface it sounds like a village team that only turns out sometimes; underneath, one word is frequency and the other is a fielder's map.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something off and on means doing it intermittently, and the two halves of a cricket field happen to carry exactly those two names.

clue.text: Demons? Companions, run away!

indicators.note: Something sent away leaves the place it was in, and what leaves here is a single letter rather than a person.

parts.note: the companions you choose are your friends
R is cricket's abbreviation for a run — this is the letter that goes

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark sells 'run away!' as panic, and it is really an instruction to a single letter. Companions and demons are about as far apart as a surface can stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Devils and evil spirits are demons by another name, and the answer is the plural that matches the plural in the clue.

clue.text: Wearing white, England finally get 500 with sweep

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so the word for white goes round these letters

parts.note: pale means white

indicators.note: finally means take the last letter of England

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500

explanation.surface: An England batsman in cricket whites reaches 500 with a sweep shot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is cricket, where players wear white and the sweep is a shot; the paddle is a variant of it.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket a paddle is a delicate sweep shot, played fine behind the batter.

clue.text: Stop going both ways?

parts.note: a word for stop that reads the same forwards and backwards

explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated phrase for halting a vehicle is a palindrome: read up or down this entry, it spells the same thing, which is what the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: To pull up is to stop a vehicle or a horse, as in pulling up at the lights.

clue.text: One in court sent in criminal to get shot

indicators.note: criminal means bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted

parts.note: taken as written
a ball is a shot, as in a cannonball

explanation.surface: A defendant in court is sent in after a criminal is shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court' suggests a law court, which the criminal fits; it is a tennis court.
explanation.definitionFit: A tennis ball is the object that is hit back and forth on a tennis court.

clue.text: Society backing favourite way to go up in the world

definitions.text: way to go up in the world

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the word for favourite is read the other way

parts.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: High society supports a favoured route to social advancement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns PET round, and it follows S.
explanation.definitionFit: A step lets you climb, and figuratively a step up is a move to higher status.

clue.text: Wide initially given following batting side

indicators.note: It asks for an opening letter, and it is doing that job for the word on each side of it rather than only the one before it.

parts.note: the initial of Wide
the batting team in cricket is the team that is in
the initial letter of the first of these two words, and the second says where it goes: behind what has just been built

explanation.walkthrough: Cricket runs right through the surface: a wide is given by the umpire, and the batting side is 'in'. The definition is the single word doing no cricket at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A wing is a side — of a building, of an army, of a football pitch — the flank rather than the centre of the thing.

clue.text: Creature of indeterminate gender?

parts.note: W is the label for women, on a form or a changing-room door
when it is not settled which of two, the two are joined by this little word
M is the matching label for men, so one word supplies both letters

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as three chunks and it says 'W or M', the two boxes on a form. Worms really are hermaphrodite, so the surface is true as well as funny.
explanation.definitionFit: A worm is an animal, if a lowly one, so 'Creature' defines it in the vaguest way available — the work of the clue is all in the wordplay.

clue.text: Perhaps Hamlet seizes Claudius's crown in play

indicators.note: To seize is to grab hold of something, and what is grabbed ends up held inside the grip.

parts.note: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, so he is one example of a Dane — 'perhaps' is the flag that says by example

indicators.note: A crown sits on top of a head, so it points at a first letter — loosely, since in an across entry nothing is really above anything else.

parts.note: the letter Claudius begins with

explanation.walkthrough: Claudius really does seize the crown in the play, so the surface reads as plot summary. The crown the wordplay wants is one letter of a usurper's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Light dances on water the way it plays on it: both verbs describe quick flickering movement, which is the sense that makes them swappable.

clue.text: 'Beats drinking alcohol' — aristocrat on reflection with slice of lemon

indicators.note: something drinking takes liquid inside it, so the alcohol goes within the reversed aristocrat
a reflection in a mirror is reversed, so the aristocrat's title is read backwards

parts.note: a lord is a member of the nobility
rum is an alcoholic spirit

indicators.note: a slice is a small piece, here just the opening letter of lemon

parts.note: the first letter of lemon, the thin slice taken off it

explanation.surface: A slogan that beats are better than booze, attached to a nobleman with a lemon slice in his drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beats' looks like a verb meaning defeats, but it is the plural noun; the quotation marks dress the definition up as a slogan.
explanation.definitionFit: A drumroll is a rapid succession of strokes on a drum, a series of beats.
